title: Shopping at the supermarket — the "with" ending
goal: Do your everyday shopping, and master the *-val / -vel* ending that melts into the consonant before it.
bekal: answer *Kivel?* and *Mivel?* with the right pronoun form

notes: **Tejjel, kenyérrel, kártyával — all the same ending.** The base form is *-val / -vel*, but the *v* disappears after a consonant and that consonant doubles. *tej* + *vel* → *tejjel*; *kenyér* + *vel* → *kenyérrel*; *kártya* + *val* → *kártyával* (after a vowel the *v* stays).

**Isszuk is the definite form of iszik.** This is one of the most irregular verbs in Hungarian: *iszom, iszod, issza, isszuk, isszátok, isszák*. Because the coffee is definite (*a kávét*), the definite form is used — the unit 11 rule still applies, however badly the verb behaves.

**Nálad lista van** uses the *-nál* ending from unit 12 to mean "on you", "do you have it with you". This pattern is very common: *Van nálad pénz?* (Do you have any money on you?), *Nincs nálam telefon* (I don't have my phone with me).

**Feketén** is the adverb of *fekete*. For coffee it means without milk — just like "black coffee" in English. The ending *-n / -an / -en* turns an adjective into an adverb, as you've seen in *jól*, *szépen*, *gyorsan*.

**Kivel and mivel are question words with an ending already on.** *Ki* + *vel* → *kivel* (with whom), *mi* + *vel* → *mivel* (with what). Hungarian question words really do take endings like ordinary nouns: *kinek* (to whom), *kitől* (from whom), *hova* (where to).

grammars.title: The -val / -vel ending: the melting v
body: The only Hungarian ending that truly changes shape to match the consonant before it. The rule is simple and has no exceptions.
after: This ending covers three meanings at once: **together with** (*Annával megyek* — I'm going with Anna), **using** (*kártyával fizetek* — I'm paying by card), and **by (transport)** (*busszal megyek* — I'm going by bus).
Note that this ending also follows vowel harmony: *-val* for back-vowel words, *-vel* for front-vowel words. So *vonattal* but *kenyérrel*, *busszal* but *késsel*.

grammars.title: With whom? Pronoun forms
body: Personal pronouns don't take the ordinary endings; they have their own forms to memorize.
after: Notice the pattern: the endings are exactly the possessive endings from unit 5 (*-m, -d, -a/-e, -nk, -tok, -uk*). Hungarian reuses the same toolkit throughout, and once you see it, these three columns stop feeling like three separate tables.
You've already met the second and third columns: *nekem* in units 5 and 7, *nálunk* in unit 13. Now you have all three at once.

grammars.title: Vesz — to buy
body: One of the irregular verbs you'll use most in shops.
after: The prefix *meg-* makes the action complete: *veszem a kenyeret* (I'm buying the bread) versus *megveszem a kenyeret* (I'll buy the bread, done). In shops you'll mostly hear the prefixed form.
Its partner *elad* means to sell, and *eladó* — which you met in unit 3 — means both "seller" and "for sale". A sign reading *ELADÓ* in a house window means the house is for sale.

blocks.text: Two words that often confuse newcomers: *bolt* and *üzlet* both mean shop and are interchangeable; while *ABC* — said *á-bé-cé* — is the old name for a small grocery store, and signs with those three letters still hang in many small towns.

blocks.title: Two habits that may surprise you
items: **Plastic bags cost money** and are almost never handed out automatically. Hungarians bring a *vászontáska* — a cloth bag — and the question *Kér zacskót?* at the checkout means you'll be charged for one.

**You weigh produce yourself** in many supermarkets: put the fruit or vegetables on the scale, press the button with the picture, and stick on the price label. The cashier won't weigh it for you, and the line behind you will soon let you know.
